title: Stack (LIFO)
description: Push, pop, peek, overflow and underflow on the bounded array-backed stack used by stack.html.

questions.prompt: You push 4, then 7, then 9 onto an empty stack, then call pop(). Which value is removed?
choices: Nothing: pop needs to be told which value to remove
questions.explanation: A stack is Last-In, First-Out: pop always removes the most recently pushed value still on the stack, which is 9. 4 is the tempting wrong answer if you think of a queue (First-In, First-Out); in a stack 4 sits at the bottom and comes out last.
questions.page: On stack.html: allocate capacity 6, push 4, 7 and 9, then type 9 in the value box and press Pop.

questions.prompt: peek() removes the top element and returns it.
questions.explanation: peek() only reads the top value; the size and top index stay the same. Removing and returning the top value is what pop() does. Mixing the two up is the most common stack mistake.
questions.page: On stack.html: push 5, press Peek twice, and watch Elements stay at 1.

questions.prompt: Starting from an empty stack with capacity 6: push 3, push 8, pop, push 5. List the stack from bottom to top.
questions.hint: Write the stack down after every operation. pop removes whatever was pushed most recently.
questions.explanation: After push 3 and push 8 the stack is [3, 8] with 8 on top. pop removes 8 (the newest value), leaving [3]. push 5 puts 5 on top: [3, 5]. Answering "3, 8, 5" forgets that pop removed something; answering "8, 5" removes the oldest value, which is queue behaviour.
questions.page: On stack.html: push 3, push 8, Pop, push 5.

questions.prompt: A stack has capacity 3. You push 1, 2, 3 and then 4. What is the top index afterwards? (The bottom slot is index 0.)
questions.hint: What happens to a push when every slot is already used?
questions.explanation: Pushing 1, 2 and 3 fills indices 0, 1 and 2, so top is 2. The push of 4 is rejected with a stack overflow and changes nothing, so top stays 2. Answering 3 assumes the stack grew, but this stack has a fixed capacity.
questions.page: On stack.html: allocate capacity 3, push 1, 2, 3, then try to push 4.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of push on this array-backed stack (which has a fixed capacity)?
questions.explanation: push writes one value at index top + 1 and increments top. That is the same amount of work whether the stack holds 1 element or 11, so it is O(1). O(n) would only apply if every existing element had to move, as it would when inserting at the front of an array.

questions.prompt: Using only push, pop and peek, how long does it take in the worst case to find out whether a value x is stored anywhere in a stack of n elements?
questions.explanation: Only the top is visible, so in the worst case (x is at the bottom or missing) you must pop all n elements to look at each one, which is O(n). O(1) is tempting because push, pop and peek are each O(1), but a search needs up to n of those steps. O(log n) would need sorted, randomly accessible data, as in binary search.

questions.prompt: Which of these operations take O(1) time on this stack? Select all that apply.
choices: Listing every element from top to bottom
questions.explanation: push, pop and peek touch only the top slot, and isFull compares size with capacity; each costs the same no matter how many elements are stored. Listing every element has to visit all n elements, so it is O(n), not O(1).

questions.prompt: A stack with capacity 4 already holds 4 values. What happens when you push 10?
choices: The push is rejected as a stack overflow and the stack is unchanged
The bottom value is dropped to make room for 10
The capacity grows to 5 and 10 is pushed
questions.answer: The push is rejected as a stack overflow and the stack is unchanged
questions.explanation: This stack has a fixed capacity. When it is full, push fails with "Stack overflow: all 4 slots are used, so 10 cannot be pushed." and nothing changes. Growing the capacity is what a dynamic array does, but this visualizer models a bounded stack. Dropping the bottom value would be a ring buffer, not a stack.
questions.page: On stack.html: allocate capacity 4, push four values, then push 10.

questions.prompt: In this visualizer, top is the index of the last element, so top is -1 when the stack is empty.
questions.explanation: top equals size − 1. With one element top is 0, and with no elements it is −1, which is why the page says "The stack is now empty (top = −1)" after the last pop. Saying top is 0 when empty would make an empty stack look the same as a stack with one element.
questions.page: On stack.html: push one value, type that value in the value box, press Pop, and read the message.

questions.prompt: The values 1, 2, 3, 4 are pushed in that order, and pops may happen at any time between the pushes. Which pop order is IMPOSSIBLE?
questions.hint: To pop 3 first, 1 and 2 must already be on the stack. Which of them is on top?
questions.explanation: To pop 3 first you must push 1, 2, 3 and pop 3. Now 2 is on top of 1, so the next pop must give 2 (or you push 4). Popping 1 next is impossible. The others are possible: 2, 1, 4, 3 (push 1, push 2, pop, pop, push 3, push 4, pop, pop); 3, 2, 4, 1 (push 1–3, pop, pop, push 4, pop, pop); 1, 2, 3, 4 (pop straight after each push).

questions.prompt: Which of these problems are naturally solved with a stack? Select all that apply.
choices: Checking that brackets like ( [ { } ] ) are balanced
Remembering where to return to when functions call other functions
Serving print jobs in the order they arrived
answer: Checking that brackets like ( [ { } ] ) are balanced
Remembering where to return to when functions call other functions
questions.explanation: Bracket matching, undo and the call stack all need the most recent unfinished item first: the latest open bracket must close first, the latest edit is undone first, and the most recently called function returns first. Print jobs served in arrival order are First-In, First-Out, which is a queue, not a stack.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the postfix expression 5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 - with a stack: push numbers, and for an operator pop b, pop a, then push a op b. What value is left on the stack?
questions.explanation: 5 1 2 → [5, 1, 2]. + pops 2 and 1 and pushes 3 → [5, 3]. 4 → [5, 3, 4]. * → [5, 12]. + → [17]. 3 → [17, 3]. - pops b = 3 and a = 17 and pushes 17 − 3 = 14. Getting −14 means the operands were popped in the wrong order: the first value popped is the RIGHT operand.

questions.prompt: In this visualizer, calling pop() on an empty stack returns null.
questions.explanation: pop() on an empty stack fails as a stack underflow: it returns an error result (ok: false) and the page shows an underflow message. It is peek() that returns null on an empty stack, because peek is only a question ("what is on top?"), while pop is a request to remove something that does not exist.
questions.page: On stack.html: allocate a capacity, then press Pop and then Peek on the empty stack.

questions.prompt: You reverse an array of n values by pushing every value onto a stack and then popping them all back into the array. What is the total time?
questions.explanation: There are n pushes and n pops, each O(1), so the total is 2n constant-time steps, which is O(n). O(n²) would mean each push or pop cost O(n), but they only touch the top slot.

questions.prompt: On stack.html, which capacity does Allocate Capacity reject?
questions.explanation: The page accepts a whole-number capacity from 1 to 12, so 13 is rejected with a message. 1 is allowed: a one-slot stack is valid, and pushing a second value simply overflows. 12 is the largest allowed value, so it is accepted.
questions.page: On stack.html: type 13 into Capacity and press Allocate Capacity.

questions.prompt: On stack.html the top value is 8. You type 5 in the value box and press Pop. What happens?
choices: Nothing is removed: the page explains that the top element is 8, not 5
5 is found and removed from the middle of the stack
8 is popped anyway and 5 is ignored
questions.answer: Nothing is removed: the page explains that the top element is 8, not 5
questions.explanation: A stack can only remove its top. Pop asks you to type the top value first and checks that it matches the top. Because 8 ≠ 5, the page shows "LIFO Rule: Top element is 8, not 5." and leaves the stack alone. Removing 5 from the middle would break LIFO; type 8 to pop the top.
questions.page: On stack.html: push 5, push 8, type 5 and press Pop.
